article.title: Black Hat Researchers Find Critical Flaws in Claude Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenAI Codex That Let a Single GitHub Issue Reach CI Secrets
article.summary: Novee Security found that a stranger's GitHub issue could reach CI runner secrets in Anthropic's, Google's, and OpenAI's own coding-agent repositories.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Security researcher Elad Meged of [Novee Security](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) disclosed at Black Hat USA on [August 5](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-coding-agent-cicd-secrets-20260808-csa/) that a GitHub issue opened by an account with no repository privileges was enough to reach CI runner secrets in the coding-agent repositories that Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI run for their own tools. Novee tested each vendor's agent against the vendor's own default configuration — [Claude Code Action on anthropics/claude-code, Gemini CLI on google-gemini/gemini-cli, and Codex on openai/codex](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) — and found paths to remote code execution, credential theft, and persistent instruction hijacking in all three.

## What We Know

In Anthropic's Claude Code, the flaw took three rounds of patch and bypass to fully close. Novee found that Claude Code's command validator [strips single-quoted text out of a command string before running its 23 validation checks](https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html), a step that is correct for how bash itself interprets quoting but that let a malicious payload smuggled inside the value of git's `--receive-pack` flag reach the runner uninspected, giving an attacker code execution and access to the workflow's tokens. Anthropic's first patch closed that hole, but Novee's second round found that a hardcoded list classifying commands such as `tac`, `rev`, `fold`, `expand`, and `unexpand` as "read-only" let those commands [bypass the path checks](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) applied to other file reads, allowing arbitrary file access on the runner. The third and final variant, tracked as [CVE-2026-54316](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54316), abused Claude Code's pre-approved outbound access to Hugging Face: because the domain was allowed as a bare hostname for the WebFetch tool, an attacker could have Claude [create up to 64 model repositories, one per possible character of a secret, and read the public download counters on those repositories as a covert channel](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) to exfiltrate an API key one character at a time. According to the National Vulnerability Database, the flaw affected [Claude Code from version 0.2.54 until 2.1.163](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54316), where it was fixed. NVD scored it 9.1 under CVSS v3.1, while Anthropic's own CVSS v4 assessment rated it 6.0, a divergence [Cloud Security Alliance's research note](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-coding-agent-cicd-secrets-20260808-csa/) attributes to differing scoring methodologies between the two scales.

Google's Gemini CLI carried the more severe of the disclosed bugs. The [GitHub Security Advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g) describes two combined issues: earlier versions "automatically trusted workspace folders in CI environments, potentially enabling remote code execution via malicious environment variables in `.gemini/` directories when processing untrusted content," and separately, when configured in `--yolo` mode, "the tool allowlist was ignored, potentially permitting arbitrary command execution via prompt injection with untrusted inputs." Novee's own account adds that the allowlist was only checked when a tool was registered and never enforced at the point of execution, so the restriction existed in name only, and that a separate design gap let an attacker [read the parent process's environment variables through Linux's `/proc/$PPID/environ` interface](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) even though the sanitized child-process environment looked clean. Google rated the combined flaw 10.0, the maximum possible score, and the fix — [`@google/gemini-cli` 0.39.1 and `run-gemini-cli` 0.1.22](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wpqr-6v78-jr5g) — went beyond a narrow patch to what Google called a breaking change to how non-interactive, headless environments handle folder trust. Novee's writeup notes the repository has [roughly two million monthly installs downstream](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/).

OpenAI's Codex produced a different outcome: no CVE and no version patch, because OpenAI concluded the underlying behavior was working as documented. Novee found that [openai/codex's own issue-triage workflow ran two Codex passes inside a single job sharing one checked-out workspace](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/), so the first pass — reading an attacker's issue text — could write to `AGENTS.md`, the default instruction file Codex loads from disk and treats as authoritative on every invocation. When the first pass's output failed schema validation, that failure was exactly what triggered a second pass, which then loaded the attacker-controlled `AGENTS.md` as its own instructions. [The Hacker News reported](https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html) that OpenAI's current workflow now separates the two passes into different jobs with independent checkouts and runs Codex with a read-only sandbox, and that OpenAI's guidance lists repository instruction files among content that "should be considered part of the untrusted input surface." Novee says OpenAI hardened its own repository within three days of the report.

Across all three vendors, Novee frames the common failure as sitting in what it calls the "harness" — the code between the model and the systems it acts on — rather than in the underlying model's behavior. "The harness is the code between the model and the real world," Meged wrote, a description [Cloud Security Alliance's research note also quotes](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-coding-agent-cicd-secrets-20260808-csa/) in attributing it to him. Novee's writeup states that comparable default configurations were found running unmodified across [well over a hundred other public repositories](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/), and separately notes [a hundred and fourteen repositories running the same issue-triggered pattern](https://novee.security/blog/critical-flaws-in-anthropic-google-and-openais-coding-agents/) it used to demonstrate the Gemini CLI chain specifically.

Cloud Security Alliance's research note adds that the Gemini CLI vulnerability was [independently discovered and reported through Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program by both Meged and Dan Lisichkin of Pillar Security](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-coding-agent-cicd-secrets-20260808-csa/). The Hacker News reported that as of August 7, [neither the Claude Code nor the Gemini CLI vulnerability appeared in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog](https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html), meaning no confirmed active exploitation had been recorded.

## What We Don't Know

Because OpenAI treated the Codex finding as intended sandbox behavior rather than a defect, no advisory or version identifier exists to tell other organizations running a similar multi-pass, shared-checkout workflow that they remain exposed; Novee's writeup states only that OpenAI's own repository was hardened within three days, not that the underlying pattern was eliminated from the product itself. It is also not established how many of the "well over a hundred" other public repositories Novee identified have since been patched or reconfigured, since that count reflects Novee's scan at the time of disclosure rather than a tracked, ongoing figure.

## Analysis

The three vendors reached three different remediation postures for structurally similar bugs. Anthropic and Google issued version patches and, in Google's case, a breaking change to a core trust assumption; OpenAI classified its finding as documented behavior and fixed only its own repository's workflow configuration, leaving the underlying multi-pass pattern — which Novee notes OpenAI's own `codex-action` tooling makes easy for other teams to copy — without a vendor-side patch path. That split illustrates a distinction the research surfaces repeatedly: agent "harness" code, the integration layer connecting a model's output to real shell commands, network calls, and file writes, is where each of the three chains ultimately succeeded, not in any model's willingness to follow a malicious instruction embedded in an issue or pull request.
